title: Chet
hookLine: with yud it spells chai, life

cards: The speeches are over. Somebody's uncle talked a little too long, the bride's friend made everyone cry, and now the glasses go up: wine, whiskey, sparkling water, whatever's in hand.
The whole table says one word together: l'chaim! Glasses touch. At Jewish weddings, at a bris, at a new job, even after a funeral when the family sits down to eat, that's the word.
It means to life. And the word for life starts with a sound you make at the back of your throat.

teach.b: You met l'chaim in year three, raised at tables after mourning; today, the letter inside it. First, its look. Chet is a cousin of heh, the breath letter.

Heh has a small gap at the top left, as if air can still slip out. Chet closes the gap: two legs and a roof, sealed. The sound changes too: not an easy h, but breath pushed against the back of the throat, ch.
Put chet beside a yud, a tiny hanging stroke, and you have chai: alive, living. Its plural, chayim, is the everyday word for life. L'chaim simply means to life.
Third, a sentence that gives the word weight. Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses lays out the choice before the people.
In the King James: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life." Not just enjoy it. Choose it, as if life were something you keep picking up, day after day.
Tradition gives each Hebrew letter a number, and says chet and yud together add up to eighteen. So some people give gifts in multiples of eighteen, and some wear chai on a chain around their neck.
And l'chaim isn't only for weddings. Over coffee with a friend you haven't seen in a while, it's a way of noticing, out loud, that you're both still here.

how: At Jewish celebrations, from weddings to a meal after a hard day, people raise a glass and say l'chaim, 'to life'; some give gifts in multiples of eighteen, the number tradition assigns to chai, and some wear the word chai as a pendant.

o: the letter that stands for the number seven
the throaty letter that helps spell chai, alive
the soft h letter heard in hallelujah

s: chet and heh look completely different
they're cousins: heh has a small gap at the top left, chet closes it.
chayim is life; the toast is said at weddings and at other tables.
Moses says it in Deuteronomy: "therefore choose life."

games.q: you're Moses, near the end of the road, laying out life and death, blessing and curse before the people. what do you tell them?
o: life and death are out of your hands.
games.why: "therefore choose life." the text treats life as something you choose, not only something that happens to you.

practice: Hold a cup if one is near, water or tea, anything, and bring to mind one thing in your life that's alive right now: a person, a friendship, a plant on the windowsill, a project finally growing.
Lift the cup a little toward it, say l'chaim under your breath, and sip slowly; if you pray, give thanks for it.

wordCard.voice: Chet. The throaty letter that, with a yud beside it, spells chai: alive, life. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: alive, living; chet (ח) plus yud (י). The toast l'chaim (לְחַיִּים) means to life.

carryVoice: Your line: chet for life. Life is something you can choose again. See you at tet.

sources.q: I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life
